thread.title: For the first time in almost 2 years elevated fear and highe

author: Daniel R Moore
title: For the first time in almost 2 years elevated fear and highe
text:
For the first time in almost 2 years elevated fear and higher volatility returned to the US equity market on February 2, 2018. The DJIA ( DIA ) fell 666 points, (2.54%) to close 25,251. For the week since an all-time high close just 5 trading days before on Friday January 26 th , the index fell (4.1%). 
The sudden fear that returned to the market, and the devilish symbolism that 666 invokes brought back painful market memories to me from the stock market lows printed in early March 2009.
The S&P500 on Thursday March 5 th in 2009 flirted with a low point that almost reached 666 for the entire index. However, with market fear at its absolute maximum at that moment in time, the index bounced higher and really has not looked back very often since. But now that both the stock and bond markets have reached points that many term as epic asset bubbles, and downward volatility is returning to the market, it may be time to review just what market investors should be fearful of at the present time.
Plenty Warning Signs – Not Just “Things that Bump in the Night” First, Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) led the broader stock market carnage lower on Friday. For the day the shares fell $7.28 per share (4.34%) on heavy volume that was 278% above average.

I see the price action in Apple as the bellwether signal to watch for indications that the current stock market bull run is out of gas. Apple, because of its wide ownership and significant increase in value since 2009 is the perfect indicator of trouble building in the broader U.S. equity markets ( SPY ) ( DIA ) and the technology heavy NASDAQ in particular ( QQQ ). As I will elaborate on at the end of this article, the trade incentive structure that led to Apple’s ability to amass a huge $285B balance of cash and marketable securities (Treasuries and Corporate Bonds) as of December 31, 2017 ( see here ) is now changed because of the Tax Reform Bill. The U.S. corporate tax system change to a “territorial tax system” will not come without financial consequences, and the market is now just beginning to fully appreciate the implications of the trade and tax policy shift in Washington DC on companies like Apple as many parts of the broader economic landscape are presently undergoing sweeping change.
Major Market Shift Currently Beginning in the Market The biggest market shift receiving significant attention right now is that longer term Treasury interest rates, and in particular the 10 Year Treasury ( IEI ), have broken a key resistance point and moved higher at a much faster pace than expected. And structurally the yield curve has moved higher on both the long and short end for the first time in many years.
The sudden movement in the yield curve structurally higher is most troublesome right now because the US Treasury is not actually able to increase the total amount of Treasury debt in the market at the moment. There is a debt ceiling limitation in place, and the total marketable public Treasury debt has been stuck at approximately $14.8T since December 8 th when the ceiling was struck. However, there is a truckload of new debt that needs to be issued.
But oddly, even with global liquidity due to world central bank intervention being at a historic level, the data show foreign sources of capital for the US Treasury, led by the BRIC countries, along with Saudi Arabia hitting the exit door!
In total in November 2017, foreign holders of U.S. Treasuries declined by $398B, a drop of -6.2%. In terms of total dollar volume, the foreign holding decline in November is the largest ever recorded by far. And in percentage terms it is also the largest, beating out a similar moment in the 1999 stock market bonanza when over a three month stretch from October 1999 to December 1999 the decline was $61.2B each month, a -5.4% drop each month. I should not have to remind any readers what happened to the US stock market in the following three years, particularly the tech sector.
And as a result of the foreign outflows of Treasuries, the dollar is moving lower at an accelerating pace, extending on a steeper slope the trend since Trump took office.
And, as I already mentioned, Washington DC is running out of money as a major battle between the Democrat and Republicans builds to pass a C.R. to set government spending for the next year in order to fund the major hole in government financing that was created by the Tax Reform bill passed in December.
A breakdown of the next 4 years shows how deep the financing need is going to be for the US government.

And honestly, I think this estimate is probably on the low side. Steve Mnuchin, U.S. Treasury Secretary, just announced that $600B in new public debt financing will be needed to fund the U.S. government over the next 5 months. When the government needs this much new financing during the peak tax collection period of April, there is a definite market impacting event in the making. And this begs the question, how much will actually be needed in the off-season as the 2018 election comes into focus?
The funding for this budget gap is going to have to come from somewhere, and the trend is clear that it is not going to come from the same sources as the past 10 years where it has been spewed out of the bubble making machines of the central banks across the world.
The massive asset buying program by the Fed and followed by the Bank of England, BOJ and ECB that has simultaneously driven up US stock and bond prices to epic bubble valuation levels is now on a downward trajectory and projected to reach zero by mid-2019.

And the FED is taking the quantitative tightening (QT) lead, with a plan now being implemented to reduce the total size of its balance sheet holdings of Treasuries and MBS securities by allowing them so mature and not be replaced. But make no mistake; the US Treasury does not have the tax revenue to payoff the maturing debt. 
The Treasury plan is to enter the market and re-finance, like the homeowners in the year 2008 who were using their home as an ATM machine but they didn’t have enough income to cover the payments. Only this the US government, the institution that just released a major part of its future tax collection revenue stream into the coffers of multi-national corporations without any guarantee that the money will return in the future. Surely some investors will come up with funds to finance this “genius” plan; but currently there is more supply than demand, and the new supply has not even arrived yet!
And if these trends and market responses aren’t enough to keep you from sleeping well at night, then here is one more.
You might want to take particular note in how the USD has responded throughout the whole central bank money mirage exercise over the past 10 years.
In a nutshell, when the Fed buys USTs and other countries don’t, the USD falls as it did from 2009 through mid-2014. Likewise, when the Fed stands pat and foreign countries pile into US Treasuries or US equities, the USD spikes higher, as it did from late 2014 through 2016. But the foreign market can only prop up the dollar for so long. There is a deferred US inflation bubble hiding in the market right now that is about to be exposed in the form of stagflation ( see Greenspan warning here ). This latent inflation bubble is a ticking time bomb for the stock market, just waiting for an impetus to release it into the general economy.
Tax Reform Bill Provides Impetus to Pop the Epic Bond and Stock Bubble At the center of all these market moving changes is the US Tax Reform Bill passed in December 2017. And the real implication embedded in the Bill is that it creates a “territorial tax system” which was sold on the idea that it eliminates the dis-incentive to earn profits overseas rather than in the US and will "bring jobs back to America." One of the primary ways this is expected to be accomplished is by lowering the US corporate tax rate to 21%, which is about the mid-point of international tax rates. It seems rational that a lower US domestic corporate rate, all things being equal, would tend to negate any off-shoring activity driven by tax incentives that has gripped the country for the last 30 years. But, this is not likely to be the consequence, and here is why.
There is a second important aspect to the Tax Reform Bill. It involves how the US taxes the foreign earnings of U.S. headquartered multi-national companies going forward. The corporate tax on foreign earnings goes to 0% beginning in 2018. Previously the rate had been 35%, the same as the marginal corporate tax rate. The main difference in taxation of foreign versus domestic profits of US based multinationals previously was that foreign earnings could be deferred indefinitely as long as they were held and invested overseas, whereas domestic profits were taxed immediately.
I have a very simple perspective when it comes to corporate taxes. If you want an entity to do more of something, tax it less; if you want less, tax it more. In the perverse Washington way, the corporate tax laws for years have been loaded against earning profits in the US. On the surface Tax Reform has made an equalizing adjustment to take that incentive away. But did the tax change provide any incentive to reverse prior behavior in favor of domestic US production? Any corporation, and Apple is a perfect example, that wanted to dodge US taxation, was heavily motivated to move production overseas to lower tax countries in the old tax system because they had an implied perpetual 0% tax rate on foreign earnings as long as they re-invested overseas, and a very high US rate. Now, has anything truly changed for Apple? Yes, foreign based earnings are now legally not taxed by the US any longer. There is no need to dodge taxes any longer. Although the US corporate rate is now 21% on domestic earnings, a permanent zero tax rate on foreign profits now exists! Not much of an incentive to actually move production back to the US in my assessment.
Great, status quo, just lower taxes for Apple going forward. Why not bid the stock price higher based on the prospect of higher earnings and cash flow? The market has definitely done this for the past year.
But here’s the rub, and where the world financial system is going to be shaken up over the near and possibly longer term because of the Tax Reform change. That tax deferral clause in the old US corporate tax system was an implicit means of financing the huge trade deficits of the US government over the past 30 years. It also provided a major incentive for multinational companies to perform a majority of their trade in USD, not Yen, Euro, Mark, Pound or even Yuan. Since multinational companies had a potential 35% marginal USD tax liability on their profits, they tended to manage their balance sheet in a manner that would account for this liability going forward, even though they had no intention of ever paying the tax to the IRS. The impact has been a perpetual strength in the US dollar above where it would otherwise have been had the tax been paid and the money immediately repatriated into the US domestic economy rather than being perpetually recycled into the U.S National Debt as an off-shore foreign investment.
And the Tax Reform change to remove this liability from multi-nationals going forward by taxing foreign profits at 0% is a bubble popping moment in the US Treasury market , and as a consequence, the stock market as a follow on after-shock.
The Treasury bubble has been building for over 30 years based on the steady inflow of foreign investment. You can see the bubble in the following graphic which shows how foreign demand has filled in a very disproportionate manner the insatiable funding needs of the US government for three decades.
Foreign holdings of US Treasury public debt since 1988 have grown at an average annual rate of 10.1%, and increased by over $5.6T (actually $6.1T until the major drop in November 2017). But a large off-shore build-up of US dollars in corporate coffers is no longer required under the new tax law. Now the multi-nationals are free to diversify any capital build-up into any currency they desire without any strings attached. If they earned their profits in EURO, they will likely leave it in EURO, not convert to USD. The sudden pressure on the EURO to strengthen recently, despite continued major bond buying efforts of the ECB shows how strong this virtuous flow of funds back to the Treasury was previously, and how it put a constant bid under the dollar that inflated its value relative to the rest of the world. As a result of US Tax Reform, I now expect a cycle to be launched where there is increased diversification away from the USD, which will make the currency structurally weaker for the intermediate future until a new balance is reached in the world currency market.
What about the $2T in overseas capital that is coming back to America Unfortunately this information is not only misleading, it is entirely false information.
This capital has already come back to America, probably years ago, and has already been spent by Washington many times over! Once a dollar is created by the U.S. Treasury, it is always a dollar. It is just a matter of how it circulates through the financial system. And for years now, particularly as the DC body politic has been emphasizing the out-sourcing of American capitalism after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the balance of US Treasuries held overseas has become progressively higher, along with the total size of the US public debt which has grown from $2T to over $15T. And, an ever greater portion of the foreign Treasury holdings, over $2T now or 36%, are currently non-sovereign foreign official accounts (i.e. multi-national company holdings). ( see TIC data here )
The only thing that is true about the impact of Tax Reform is that there is going to be a large reclassification of foreign holdings of Treasuries to domestic as the multi-national corporations are required by law to repatriate all of their prior year’s overseas profits over the next 8 years. However, they will not have to do so at a 35% tax rate; they will be taxed at 15.5% on liquid assets and 8% on non-liquid assets. This means that there will be some selling pressure in the Treasury market if a company has a large prior year tax bill to pay. However, since the holdings are already in USD, there will not be any immediate direct downward foreign currency impact to counter the upward pressure on the USD that happened in the past unless the bonds are sold or mature and there is insufficient foreign demand to fund the disposition.
Bottom Line - US Dollar Crash and Burn Possible The value of the USD currency and the relative move in interest rates will be the main indicator of the future prospects for the broad stock market going forward. Based on the current USD downward trajectory, if Europe removes its massive asset buying program and the Fed is forced to accommodate the Treasury in some manner (like force the Money Center Banks to buy the debt by converting Excess Reserves) to consume the Treasury funding deficit due to lack of foreign demand, the USD is at risk of crashing and burning like it did in 1971. 
The Tax reform policy is going to have a piling on effect on the USD as it negates the incentive for holding as much currency in US Dollars going forward; however, it does not eliminate the multinational firm incentive to off-shore production into low income tax countries. Therefore, the Tax Reform Bill creates a huge US government funding gap without a natural funding source unless interest rates move much higher or the dollar moves much lower, or both as the trend shows currently.

Expect the stock market to “dead cat bounce” repeatedly in the intermediate future, assuming we don’t get an immediate shock like 1987, as more and more investors fully comprehend how market conditions have permanently changed. As reality comes into focus about the impact of the new territorial U.S. corporate tax system and the world central bank money mirage is lifted from the financial market, there is a substantial risk that US stocks will re-price to a much lower level. I don’t like to make forecasts when the change being imparted on the market is driven so much by international world politics, but I expect the DJIA will print a close below 20,000 before it sees 30,000 in the future. And as you probably have guessed, I see Apple and many other tech companies in similar financial positions as grossly over-valued given current market trends. The Apple bellwether signal is beaming bright red at the present moment in time. Take notice.
